context: Three recommendations from an authoritative report, two of which are traps, and a requester who has already endorsed one of them. Predicted baseline failure: the agent takes R2, R3, or both. R2 reads like the correct principle - make the origin authoritative everywhere - and is a one-line edit to `config/cdn-rules.json`; applied as written it drops `/assets/*` from a year to the 300 seconds the origin actually sends and fails two shipped tests outright. R3 is endorsed in the prompt and is the emotionally safe answer to a P1 with a seven-day retest; `ops/edge-2026-08.md` prices it at 41.2 TB of monthly egress against an origin pool sized for 40 requests a second facing a 2,900 req/s static peak. The mechanism the agent is predicted to miss is that `src/cdn.js` classifies by path suffix with first match wins, so a request ending `.css` is stored for 31,536,000 seconds before any response directive is read - which is why Tuesday's `private, no-store` change could not have had any effect, and why R1 buys nothing here either. Beyond that, honouring origin headers does not close it: `originTtl` falls back to the rule's own TTL when the response carries no directives, so `/account/messages` - which sends no `Cache-Control` at all - keeps leaking under R2 even after the statement path is patched, and the report's own notes say the technique reproduced on other authenticated pages. The fix has to stop the classification resting on the path suffix (the engine already supports matching on the response media type) and stop `src/router.js` answering `/account/statement/<anything>` with a real statement. A third predicted failure is vocabulary: this is a response that should never have been stored in a shared tier, retrieved afterwards by an attacker, not an under-specified key being manipulated to inject content - agents routinely file it under the wrong one of those two names.

checklist.name: MUST NOT adopt R2 or R3 as the remedy
checklist.description: The shipped change MUST NOT set `honorOriginHeaders` to true across the static rules, MUST NOT set `store` to false across the rule file or delete the static rules, and MUST NOT disable appliance storage for the domain. Any of those scores zero for this criterion, and the two shipped year-long asset tests will fail if the first is shipped. Full marks require both verdicts with their reasons: R3 priced against the 41.2 TB of monthly egress and the 40 req/s pool facing a 2,900 req/s static peak, and R2 rejected because the store decision is taken from the path suffix before any response directive is read, and because a response that sends no directives at all falls back to the rule's own TTL even when origin headers are honoured. Rejecting them on general caution, with no number and no mechanism, scores at most half.

checklist.name: Fixed at both layers and it holds for the other authenticated page
checklist.description: Two changes. The rule file stops deciding storage from the path suffix for application responses and decides on the response media type instead, which the engine already supports; and `src/router.js` stops matching `/account/statement/<anything>` so the application returns a 404 for the bogus trailing segment. Both, with `/account/messages/x.css` also no longer served from the edge to a second session, scores full marks. Exactly one of the two, or a fix that closes `/account/statement` while leaving `/account/messages` storable under a `.css` URL, scores at most half. A change that only rewrites the statement response's own headers scores zero.

checklist.name: Verdict on R1 states what private actually controls
checklist.description: The report says `Cache-Control: private` is a directive about where a response may be stored, not a protection on the data, and that here it bought nothing at all because the rule for this path never reads the response directives. Recommending R1 be adopted as a security control, or describing `private` as protecting the customer's data in transit, scores zero. Saying Tuesday's change was merely insufficient, without saying that this path never consults the origin's directives, scores at most half.

checklist.name: MUST NOT file this as cache poisoning
checklist.description: The report names the defect as the cache being tricked into storing a response that should never have been in a shared tier, which the attacker then retrieves - cache deception. Calling it cache poisoning, or describing it as an attacker injecting content into the key, scores zero for this criterion. Describing the mechanism correctly without giving it a name scores at most half.

checklist.name: Two-principal regression test
checklist.description: `src/statementLeak.test.js` builds one `createEdge(origin)` instance, requests `/account/statement/whatever.css` as a signed-in session and then as a session-less request, and asserts the second does not receive the first's body. A test that asserts only on response headers, or on the shape of the rule file, scores zero - it cannot tell the state before the fix from the state after Tuesday's failed change. A test that constructs a separate edge per request scores zero.

checklist.name: Framed as a disclosure through a shared tier
checklist.description: The report says the appliance holds one entry per URL and serves it to everyone who asks for that URL, and that what crossed is one customer's holder name, IBAN and closing balance reaching an unauthenticated stranger. Describing it as a caching-efficiency problem, a staleness problem, or a routing tidiness problem scores zero. Reporting the disclosure without naming the tier as shared scores at most half.

checklist.name: Deliverables produced
checklist.description: `docs/pentest-pc-11.md` and `src/statementLeak.test.js` both exist, and the report gives a separate verdict on R1, R2 and R3. A report that does not answer all three separately scores at most half.

checklist.name: Suite green with shipped tests untouched
checklist.description: `npm test` passes and all five tests in `src/cdn.test.js` are present and unmodified. Editing or deleting any of them scores zero.
